Austria
AWS-tree-a
n. (the Habsburg hereditary lands on the Danube, largely Lutheran by 1570 and wholly recatholicised by 1700)
Latin Austria, from Old High German Ostarrîchi, the eastern realm; German Österreich.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Austria is the land where the Reformation won the people and lost the prince, and where losing the prince proved to be decisive. By the 1570s the great majority of the Austrian nobility and of the burghers of Vienna, Linz and the Danube towns were Lutheran; the estates obtained the Religious Concession of 1568 and the Pacification of 1571, which allowed evangelical worship on noble estates, and Lutheran preaching was heard in Vienna within sight of the emperor's palace. There was no Austrian reformed church order, no Austrian confession and no Austrian synod; the evangelical cause rested on the estates' bargaining power and on preachers whom individual lords employed. When Ferdinand II came to the hereditary lands he dissolved it piece by piece: preachers expelled from 1598, reformation commissions with troops behind them, the nobility required after 1627 to conform or sell and emigrate, and the peasants left to be catechised by Jesuits. Tens of thousands left. Those who stayed became the crypto-Protestants of the Alpine valleys, keeping forbidden books for five generations until the Patent of Toleration of 1781 let them register. The dictionary enters Austria because it is the clearest case of a reformation that depended on patronage and was dismantled when the patrons were bought out.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a patent as a writing granting a privilege; to conform as to comply with or yield obedience; emigration as removal from one country to another; and toleration as the allowance by law of religious opinions.

expand to see more

PATENT, n. A writ or writing granting a privilege, or authenticating a right or title; letters patent.

CONFORM, v. To comply with or yield obedience to; to be obedient or submissive; to make like in manners or opinions.

EMIGRATION, n. Removal of inhabitants from one country or state to another, for the purpose of residence.

TOLERATION, n. The allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, when contrary to those of the established church.

PATRON, n. A protector; a supporter; one who countenances or supports another.

Modern Corruption

The Habsburg hereditary lands, largely Lutheran by 1570 under noble patronage, recatholicised by commission and emigration patent after 1598.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the church held by patronage, which is a landlord's church and falls with the landlord. Austria had evangelical preaching for two generations without ever building what Saxony and Scotland built: a confession the common people had learned, a catechising ministry in every parish, a synod able to meet and act. When Ferdinand required the nobility to conform or to emigrate, and most emigrated, the structure went with them, because the structure was their household chaplaincies. “the LORD shall scatter thee among all people” (Deu 28:64) came true in a land that had thought itself safe by treaty.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the crown is not the church's foundation, and that he who gives the crown takes it away. “he removeth kings, and setteth up kings” (Dan 2:21) is the comfort of a people whose emperor has turned against them, and the Austrian crypto-Protestants lived on it for five generations with their books hidden in barns. Of them, as of the exiles who went down the Danube with what they could carry, it is written that “they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew puts (H6327), to scatter; Greek nikao (G3528), to overcome; Hebrew melek (H4428), a king.

expand to see more

Hebrew puts (H6327) — to scatter, to disperse abroad; “the LORD shall scatter thee among all people”, Deuteronomy 28:64.

Greek nikao (G3528) — to conquer, to overcome, to prevail; “they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb”, Revelation 12:11.

Greek marturia (G3141) — a testimony borne, a witness; “the word of their testimony”, Revelation 12:11.

Greek planao (G4105) — to wander, to be led astray; “they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins”, Hebrews 11:37.

Aramaic melek (H4430) — a king, a sovereign; “he removeth kings, and setteth up kings”, Daniel 2:21.

Usage

"“the LORD shall scatter thee among all people” (Deu 28:64) — the emigration patent laid on the nobility after 1627."

"“they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11) — the crypto-Protestants of the Alpine valleys to 1781."

"“he removeth kings, and setteth up kings” (Dan 2:21) — a reformation that rested on the prince and fell with him."
